course.title: Electronics Foundations
course.description: Work out how simple direct-current circuits behave, using diagrams you can change and calculations you can check.
course.audience: A beginner using an Arduino starter kit or studying introductory electricity.

modules.title: Electric circuits
modules.description: Build a working model of how voltage drives current through a closed conducting path against resistance.

concepts.title: Electric charge
concepts.summary: Electric charge is a property of matter that produces electrical interactions.

concepts.title: Closed circuit
concepts.summary: A continuous conducting path allows charge to move around a circuit.

concepts.title: Voltage
concepts.summary: Voltage describes electric potential difference between two points.

concepts.title: Current
concepts.summary: Current measures the rate at which electric charge passes a point.

concepts.title: Resistance
concepts.summary: Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes current.

concepts.title: Ohm's law
concepts.summary: For an ohmic component, current equals voltage divided by resistance.

concepts.title: Series circuits
concepts.summary: Resistors connected in series have one path, so their equivalent resistance is the sum of their resistances.

concepts.title: Parallel circuits

concepts.title: Electrical power
concepts.summary: Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer and can be calculated for a resistor with P = IV.

concepts.title: Component behaviour
concepts.summary: A component's electrical behaviour describes how its current and voltage respond in a circuit.

lessons.title: Current in a single loop
lessons.orientation: Trace the wire from one battery terminal through the resistor until it reaches the other terminal.
lessons.explanation: Current measures how quickly electric charge passes a point in a circuit. In this single loop, the same path carries charge through the resistor and back to the battery. Ohm's law relates current to voltage and resistance: I = V / R. With 5 V and 100 Ω, the current is 0.05 A.
lessons.takeaway: Voltage supplies the push and resistance limits the flow, so the current in a single loop is the voltage divided by the resistance.

lessons.title: Resistance in series
lessons.orientation: Follow one closed path through two resistors and predict what changes when one resistor gets larger.
lessons.explanation:
In a series circuit the resistors sit one after another along a single path. Their equivalent resistance is the sum of the individual resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2. With 9 V across 100 Ω and 200 Ω, the total resistance is 300 Ω and the current is 0.03 A.

Because the path does not divide, the same current passes through both resistors. The larger resistor takes the larger share of the supply voltage: 200 Ω carrying 0.03 A drops 6 V, while 100 Ω carrying the same current drops 3 V. Those two drops add back to the 9 V the battery supplies.
lessons.takeaway: Series resistances add, the current is shared by every component in the path, and the voltage divides in proportion to each resistance.

lessons.title: When a circuit splits into branches
lessons.orientation: Look first at the two junctions in the diagram. Each resistor connects across the same pair of points, so compare the voltage across branches before considering their individual currents.
lessons.explanation:
A parallel circuit divides the path into branches. In the diagram, both resistors connect between the same two points, so each branch spans the same potential difference. With a 12 V supply, the 100 Ω branch carries 0.12 A because I = V/R, while the 300 Ω branch carries 0.04 A. These currents flow at the same time and combine in the supply path.

Adding a branch gives charge another route through the circuit. The supply then delivers more total current, and the equivalent resistance becomes smaller than the resistance of the smallest individual branch. Conductances add according to 1 / Rtotal = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2. For 100 Ω beside 300 Ω, the equivalent resistance is 75 Ω, giving a total supply current of 0.16 A from 12 V.

Use the slider explorer to change either branch resistance. Watch how lowering a branch resistance increases that branch's current and changes the total resistance. Two equal 100 Ω branches produce an equivalent resistance of 50 Ω because the available conductance doubles.
lessons.takeaway: Parallel branches share the same potential difference, while their currents add and reduce the equivalent resistance.

lessons.title: How much energy a circuit moves
lessons.orientation: Watch the calculated current as you raise the supply, and keep track of how hard the resistor is working.
lessons.explanation:
Electrical power is the rate at which a circuit transfers energy. For any component, the power is the current through it multiplied by the potential difference across it: P = IV, measured in watts. A resistor carrying 0.25 A with 6 V across it transfers 1.5 W.

Ohm's law lets the same quantity be written from whichever pair of values you already know. Substituting V = IR gives P = I²R, and substituting I = V / R gives P = V² / R. A 100 Ω resistor with 5 V across it dissipates 25 / 100 = 0.25 W.

Power says nothing on its own about how much energy has been moved. Energy is power multiplied by time, so a 0.25 W resistor left running for 60 s transfers 15 J. This matters in practice because a resistor's rating is a power rating: exceed it and the component heats until it fails.
lessons.takeaway: Power is the rate of energy transfer, P = IV, and energy is that power multiplied by the time the circuit runs.

lessons.title: Components that break the pattern
lessons.orientation: Compare what a resistor does as the voltage rises with what a light-emitting diode does over the same range.
lessons.explanation:
A resistor is ohmic: double the voltage across it and the current through it doubles, so its resistance stays constant. Plotting current against voltage for a resistor gives a straight line through the origin.

A light-emitting diode behaves differently. Below its forward voltage almost no current passes. Above that voltage the current climbs steeply for a very small increase in voltage, so the diode has no single resistance you can quote. Connect it the other way round and it blocks current altogether, which is why an LED wired backwards simply stays dark.

That steep response is what makes a series resistor necessary. Suppose a red LED with a 2 V forward voltage runs from a 5 V supply at 15 mA. The resistor has to take the remaining 3 V, so its value is 3 V / 0.015 A = 200 Ω. The resistor, not the LED, is what sets the current.
lessons.takeaway: An ohmic component keeps a constant resistance, while a diode's current rises steeply past its forward voltage and needs a series resistor to set it.

questions.prompt: A 5 V battery is connected across a 100 Ω resistor. Calculate the current in amperes.
hints: Write Ohm's law as I = V / R.
Substitute 5 V for V and 100 Ω for R.
Divide 5 by 100. Express the result in amperes.

transfer.prompt: A 6 V battery is connected across a 200 Ω resistor. Calculate the current in amperes.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery is connected to 100 Ω and 200 Ω resistors in series. Calculate the current in amperes.
hints: Add the two series resistances to find the total resistance.
Use Ohm's law with 9 V and the total resistance.
Divide 9 by 300. Express the result in amperes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rtotal = 100 Ω + 200 Ω = 300 Ω; I = V / Rtotal = 9 V / 300 Ω = 0.03 A.

questions.prompt: A 6 V battery is connected across a 150 Ω resistor. Calculate the current in amperes.
hints: Ohm's law relates the three quantities as I = V / R.
Substitute 6 V for V and 150 Ω for R.
Carry out the division and give the result in amperes.

questions.prompt: A single-loop circuit contains one battery and one resistor. Explain why the current has the same value on both sides of the resistor.
hints: Think about how many routes the charge has around this circuit.
Ask what would have to happen to the charge for the two values to differ.
Say what the single path implies about the rate of flow at any two points.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: There is only one path, so the same current passes every point in it. Charge is not used up by the resistor; the resistor limits the rate of flow rather than consuming the charge.

questions.prompt: A single-loop circuit has a fixed resistor. Which change increases the current?
hints: Write down I = V / R and look at which quantity each option changes.
Raising the denominator lowers the result; raising the numerator raises it.
Decide which option raises the numerator of I = V / R.

choices.label: Adding a second resistor along the same path
Replacing the resistor with a larger one

questions.prompt: A 220 Ω resistor and a 330 Ω resistor are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance in ohms.
hints: In a series path the resistances combine by addition.
Write Rtotal = R1 + R2 with the two given values.
Add 220 and 330, and give the result in ohms.

questions.prompt: Two unequal resistors are connected in series across a battery. Explain what this arrangement does to the current in each resistor and to the voltage across each resistor.
hints: Start from how many routes the charge has through a series pair.
Decide whether the current can differ between two components on one route.
Then say how the supply voltage is shared between unequal resistances.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two resistors sit in a single path, so the same current passes through both. The voltage divides between them, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

questions.prompt: A third resistor is added to an existing series circuit, along the same single path. What happens to the total resistance?
hints: Recall how series resistances combine.
A third resistor adds another term to that combination.
Decide whether adding a positive term raises or lowers the total.

acceptedIdeas: it rises by the value of the new resistor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises by the value of the new resistor.

choices.label: It rises by the value of the new resistor
It falls below the smallest resistance in the path
It stays the same because the path is unchanged
It becomes the average of the three resistances

questions.prompt: A resistor carries a current of 0.25 A with 6 V across it. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: Power is the product of the current through a component and the voltage across it.
Write P = IV and substitute 0.25 A and 6 V.
Multiply the two values, and give the result in watts.

questions.prompt: A 100 Ω resistor has 5 V across it. Calculate the power it dissipates, in watts.
hints: You know the voltage and the resistance, so find the current first with I = V / R.
5 V across 100 Ω gives a current you can then use in P = IV.
Alternatively use P = V² / R directly: square 5 and divide by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = 5 V / 100 Ω = 0.05 A, so P = IV = 0.05 A × 5 V = 0.25 W. Equivalently P = V² / R = 25 / 100 = 0.25 W.

questions.prompt: A 9 V supply drives 20 mA through a component. Calculate the power delivered to it, in watts.
hints: Convert the current to amperes before multiplying.
20 mA is 0.02 A.
Multiply the converted current by 9 V, and give the result in watts.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the power a resistor dissipates and the energy it transfers.
hints: One of the two quantities depends on how long the circuit runs.
Think about what has to be multiplied by time.
State the relationship between the two quantities in one sentence.

rejectedIdeas: power and energy are the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts. Energy is power multiplied by the time the circuit runs, so a 0.25 W resistor transfers 15 J in 60 s.

questions.prompt: A light-emitting diode with a forward voltage of 2 V runs from a 5 V supply at 15 mA. Calculate the resistance of the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: The diode and the resistor share the supply voltage between them.
Subtract the forward voltage from the supply voltage to find the voltage across the resistor.
Divide that voltage by the current, converting 15 mA to amperes first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 5 V − 2 V = 3 V. With 15 mA = 0.015 A, R = 3 V / 0.015 A = 200 Ω.

questions.prompt: Explain why a light-emitting diode is normally wired with a resistor in series with it.
hints: Think about how sharply the diode's current changes once its forward voltage is reached.
Ask what would set the current if the diode were the only component in the path.
State what the resistor does to the current in the branch.

rejectedIdeas: the resistor makes the diode brighter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Past its forward voltage the diode's current rises steeply for a very small voltage increase, so the diode cannot set its own working current. The series resistor takes the remaining voltage and sets the current in the branch.

questions.prompt: State what it means for a component to be ohmic, and give one example of a component that is not.
hints: Consider the shape of a graph of current against voltage.
An ohmic component gives a straight line through the origin.
Name a component whose graph is not a straight line.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An ohmic component keeps the current proportional to the voltage across it, so it has a constant resistance. A diode is not ohmic, because its current climbs steeply once the forward voltage is reached.

questions.prompt: A light-emitting diode is connected the wrong way round in a low-voltage direct-current circuit. What happens?
hints: A diode conducts in one direction only.
Think about what the reversed connection does to the current in the branch.
Decide what the learner would observe.

acceptedIdeas: almost no current flows and the diode stays dark
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Almost no current flows and the diode stays dark.

choices.label: Almost no current flows and the diode stays dark
The diode lights with the same brightness as before
The current doubles because the path is shorter
The diode lights more brightly and cools down

questions.prompt: What is the equivalent resistance of two 100 Ω branches connected in parallel?
hints: Start with the parallel conductance equation.
Substitute 100 Ω for both branch resistances.
Add the two reciprocal terms, then invert the result to obtain the resistance.

questions.prompt: A 100 Ω branch and a 300 Ω branch are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. What total current does the supply deliver?
hints: Find the current in each branch using I = V / R.
Calculate the two branch currents using 12 V and their resistances.
Add the branch currents because they flow together in the supply path.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The branch currents are 12 / 100 = 0.12 A and 12 / 300 = 0.04 A. Their sum is 0.16 A.

questions.prompt: Why is the equivalent resistance of parallel branches smaller than either branch on its own?
hints: Think about what adding a branch gives charge.
Ask what happens to the total current the supply delivers.
Relate that extra current to the resistance the supply sees.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A second branch gives charge another route, so the supply delivers more current for the same voltage. That is why the equivalent resistance is smaller than either branch.

questions.prompt: Two parallel lamps are connected across a 6 V battery. What potential difference is across each lamp?
hints: Parallel branches connect across the same two points.
Compare each branch's endpoints with the battery terminals.

rejectedIdeas: The lamps have different potential differences

choices.label: The lamps have different potential differences

flashcards.front: What does Ohm's law relate, and how is it written?
flashcards.back: For an ohmic component it fixes the current as the voltage divided by the resistance: I = V / R.

flashcards.front: What does electric current measure, and in what unit?
flashcards.back: The rate at which electric charge passes a point, measured in amperes.

flashcards.front: How is the equivalent resistance of resistors in series calculated?
flashcards.back: By adding them: Rtotal = R1 + R2, and so on for any further resistors in the path.

flashcards.front: In a series circuit, which quantity is the same in every component?
flashcards.back: The current, because a series path does not divide.

flashcards.front: How is the electrical power of a component calculated from its current and voltage?
flashcards.back: P = IV, in watts. Substituting Ohm's law also gives P = I²R and P = V² / R.

flashcards.front: What separates electrical power from electrical energy?
flashcards.back: Power is the rate of energy transfer; energy is that power multiplied by the time the circuit runs.

flashcards.front: Why does a light-emitting diode need a resistor in series with it?
flashcards.back: Its current rises steeply past the forward voltage, so the resistor takes the remaining voltage and sets the current.

flashcards.front: What does it mean to call a component ohmic?
flashcards.back: Its current stays proportional to the voltage across it, so its resistance is constant.

flashcards.front: What happens to equivalent resistance when branches are connected in parallel?
flashcards.back: It falls below the resistance of the smallest branch because the branch conductances add.

flashcards.front: What potential difference does each parallel branch have?
flashcards.back: Each branch has the same potential difference because every branch connects across the same two points.
